# The Problem

When working in R, it's already common to have standard conventions for code style: packages like [lintr](https://lintr.r-lib.org/) [@hester2025] and [styler](https://styler.r-lib.org/), and tools like [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) and [jarl](https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/) are widely used to ensure that code conforms to agreed standards. 

Documentation doesn't receive as much attention as code. 
While `R CMD check` verifies that documentation exists and matches usage, there is no common tooling for ensuring that docs are readable by a human. This responsibility falls to the authors and reviewers.

Complex and confusing documentation increases cognitive load [@sweller1988], frustrates users, and can be a real barrier to adoption and understanding.
Long sentences, unexplained jargon and a tone that assumes things are obvious all add to this.
This problem affects everyone but can be a bigger challenge for newcomers and people for whom English is not their first language.
Better documentation means wider adoption of tools, and faster onboarding of newcomers. This problem is recognised by organisations like rOpenSci, whose software review process asks reviewers to judge whether documentation is clear and sufficient [@ropensci2026].

R packages are increasingly being written with the help of, or exclusively by, AI tools. 
While many AI models are capable of writing accurate documentation, they vary in their ability to write understandable and helpful documentation.
Without any oversight, it's easy to end up with verbose and jargon-filled documentation.
This problem is only going to grow with the increased prevalence of these tools.
However, with guidance about best practice in writing for humans, in the form of documentation linting, both human and AI authors can produce better docs.

Prior work exists in the form of the [docreview](https://github.com/thisisnic/docreview) package, published on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=docreview) between 2021 and 2024. It contained 5 checks, including vignette length and readability scores, but it stalled due to the complexity of its architecture and had no path to integration with editors.

Other packages exist which cover a subset of the problem. The [spelling](https://docs.ropensci.org/spelling/) package checks words but not prose, [quanteda.textstats](https://quanteda.io/) can calculate a readability score but doesn't turn it into a rule you can run on CI, and the linters mentioned earlier only look at code. 
Outside of R, Vale [@vale] is an example of a documentation linter, with prose rules, and packaged style guides which runs in editors and on CI.  It is compatible with Quarto and other forms of markdown, and can extract the text of comments from R source files, but it has no understanding of R package structure, no vocabulary of common R terms, and no style reflecting how R package documentation is written. Its built-in styles are noisy on R code comments, flagging function and argument names as spelling errors, and using it requires installing and configuring a separate binary outside of R.

The R ecosystem lacks an opinionated documentation linter, usable from R, that can be used by both humans and AI tools to write better docs for R packages.
